papers.title_in_file: An Invertible All-optical Logic Gate on Chip
papers.what_it_is: An experimental and simulation study of an all-optical gate in a periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate microring, where quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation lets the earlier-arriving pulse act as control and the later one as signal, so the roles invert with a small change in relative delay.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrate an invertible all-optical gate on chip, in which the roles of control and signal are switchable by slightly adjusting their relative arrival time at the gate, based on quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation in a periodic-poled lithium niobate microring resonator.
quotes: We demonstrate an invertible all-optical gate on chip, with the roles of control and signal switchable by slightly adjusting their relative arrival time at the gate.
It is based on quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation in a periodic-poled lithium niobate microring resonator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical demonstration from one device in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that in transistors and switches, either electronic or optical, the roles of control and signal are fixed, and that the swappable roles of the quantum Zeno blockade gate are distinct to all existing logical gates.
quotes: In transistors and switches, either electronic or optical, the roles of control and signal are fixed [1, 2].
This is distinct to all existing logical gates, where their roles are fixed.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about prior art, supported only by two general citations.
assertions.reader_inference: The universality of the claim (all existing gates) is not argued in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, when the sum-frequency generation (SFG) induced loss is high, the cavity becomes effectively under-coupled, so the second pulse mostly does not enter the cavity, SFG nearly does not happen, and the first pulse is not affected by the second. They conclude that the first pulse always acts as the control and the second as the signal, so the roles are defined only by which pulse arrives first.
quotes: when the SFG-induced loss is so high, the cavity becomes effectively under-coupled, so that the second pulse will mostly not enter the cavity.
Therefore, the first pulse always acts as the control and the second as the signal.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative explanation given by the authors, supported by the simulation and measurements in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that the invertible all-optical logical operation is realized by adjusting the relative arrival time, which could be tens to hundreds of picoseconds.
quotes: This realizes an invertible alloptical logical operation by adjusting the relative arrival time, which could be tens to hundreds of picoseconds.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of scale; the measurements use about 300 ps and about 500 ps delays.

assertions.value: The authors state that the periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) microring is fabricated on a Z-cut 600 nm TFLN, with 80 micrometer ring radius, 1700 nm top-width and 149 poling grating number.
quotes: The periodically poled TFLN microring is fabricated on a Z-cut 600 nm TFLN, with 80 µm ring radius, 1700 nm top-width and 149 poling grating number.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own device setup, Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quasi-phase matching conditions for triple resonance use the fundamental quasi-transverse-magnetic (quasi-TM) modes, to make the best use of the largest nonlinear tensor d33. The triple resonances are identified at wavelengths of 1545.73 nm, 1558.15 nm, and 775.97 nm; the pulse trains at 1545.73 nm and 1558.15 nm are called Pulse 1 and Pulse 2.
quotes: use of the largest nonlinear tensor d33, the quasi-phase matching conditions for achieving triple resonance are the fundamental quasi-transverse-magnetic (quasi-TM) modes.
The triple resonances are identified at wavelengths of 1545.73 nm, 1558.15 nm, and 775.97 nm.
In this study, we call pulse trains at 1545.73 nm and 1558.15 as Pulse 1 and Pulse 2, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Section II.

assertions.value: The authors report that the photon-photon interaction strength g is measured to be 8.2 MHz in angular frequency, and that the quantum conversion efficiency reaches 65% when the pump is 115 microwatts.
quotes: The photon-photon interaction strength g is measured to be 8.2 MHz in angular frequency.
The quantum conversion efficiency reaches 65% when pump is 115 µW
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured value from one device; the Introduction cites the 8.2 MHz value to an earlier study [18].

assertions.value: The authors report that, in the cold cavity, all resonances are over-coupled. They report total (external) decay rates of 9.4 GHz (7.6 GHz) at 1545.73 nm, 10.1 GHz (8.5 GHz) at 1558.15 nm, and 14.1 GHz (12.1 GHz) for the sum-frequency resonance.
quotes: When it is ”cold” (at low laser intensities), the cavity’s resonances are all in the over-coupled regime.
The cold-cavity total decay rate (κt,1) for 1545.73 nm stands at 9.4 GHz, with an external decay rate (κe,1) of 7.6 GHz.
For the resonance at 1558.15 nm, the total decay rate (κt,2) is measured at 10.1 GHz, and the external decay rate (κe,2) is 8.5 GHz.
the total decay rate (κt,f ) is 14.1 GHz, and the external decay rate (κe,f ) is 12.1 GHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured device parameters from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the SFG in the nonlinear cavity is described by simplified coupled mode equations (Eqs. 1 to 3) for the photon-number amplitudes of Pulse 1, Pulse 2 and the sum-frequency wave, with detuning, total and external decay rates, interaction strength g and input photon flux. They state that the simulated outputs are calculated by solving the equations in the time domain with Matlab, using the cold-cavity parameters and the exact measured input pulses.
quotes: The SFG in the nonlinear cavity can be described by the following simplified coupled mode equations [25]:
In our simulation, the cold-cavity parameters are used
The simulated outputs are calculated by solving the (1), (2) and (3) in
time domain with Matlab.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its simulation model, Section II; the equations themselves are in the figure-like text layer and are not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pulses are Gaussian-shaped, with a 2 ns full width half maximum (FWHM) and repetition rates at the megahertz level, chosen to mitigate thermo-optic and photorefractive side effects. The pulses are carved from two tunable lasers by electro-optical modulators driven by an arbitrary waveform generator, amplified with erbium-doped fiber amplifiers and filtered by 200 GHz DWDM, and the coupling loss per facet is measured to be about 5.0 dB.
quotes: The pulses employed in the experiment are Gaussianshaped, with a 2 ns full width half maximum (FWHM) and repetition rates at the megahertz level.
This specific pulse configuration is chosen to mitigate the side effects associated with thermal-optic and photorefractive (PR) phenomena [26–28].
The coupling loss per facet is measured to be about 5.0 dB.
with a 200GHz bandwidth dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) applied afterwards
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that the measured output power of each pulse train is normalized against its measured peak power under the off-resonance condition, and that the relative arrival times are adjusted by tuning the phase of the electrical signals on the arbitrary waveform generator.
quotes: The relative arrival times of the pulses are finely adjusted by tuning the phase of the electrical signals on the AWG.
the measured output power of each pulse train is normalized against its measured peak power under the off-resonance condition
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of how its transmission percentages are computed, Section II.
assertions.reader_inference: All transmission percentages reported later are fractions of the off-resonance peak output, not of the on-chip input.

assertions.value: The authors report that at 2 mW peak power for both pulses, with Pulse 1 entering the cavity about 300 ps before Pulse 2, Pulse 2 restores its transmission to 66.2% of the off-resonance case due to QZB, while the transmission of Pulse 1 is 16.8% of that in Fig. 2(a). The output ratio between the two is 1:3.9.
quotes: This results in Pulse 2 restoring its transmission through the cavity to 66.2% of the off-resonance case due to QZB, as illustrated in Fig. 2(b).
Meanwhile, the transmission of Pulse 1 is 16.8% of that in Fig. 2(a)
While Pulse 1 and 2 have the same peak power, at the output the ratio between the two is 1:3.9.
The experimental results when the peak power for both pulses are set at 2 mW is shown in Fig. 2.
Pulse 1 (with a repetition rate of 1 MHz) is introduced into the cavity approximately 300 ps before Pulse 2
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that at 2 mW peak power, when Pulse 1 arrives roughly 300 ps after Pulse 2, the roles invert: the transmission of Pulse 1 is restored to 62.3% and that of Pulse 2 decreases to 18.2%, a power ratio of 3.4:1.
quotes: Subsequently, when Pulse 1 arrives roughly 300 ps after Pulse 2, their roles are inverted with a contrasting behavior: the transmission of Pulse 1 is restored to 62.3%, whereas that of Pulse 2 decreases to 18.2%; see Fig. 2(e).
The power ratio is now 3.4:1
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The role inversion is shown by one swap of delay at one power setting; the paper reports no repeats or error bars.

assertions.value: The authors report that at 1 mW peak power for both pulses, with the optimal arrival time difference of approximately 500 ps, when Pulse 1 precedes Pulse 2 the Pulse 1 output is 18.9% of the off-resonance case and Pulse 2 is restored to 37.8%. When Pulse 1 arrives after Pulse 2, the former is 37.8% and the latter drops to 15.5%. The power extinction ratios for these two cases are 1:2.0 and 2.4:1.
quotes: the pulse power is scaled down to 1 mW and the optimal modulation efficiency is achieved with the arrival time difference of approximately 500 ps.
When Pulse 1 precedes Pulse 2, the Pulse 1 output is at 18.9% of the off-resonance case, while Pulse 2 is restored to 37.8%, as illustrated in Fig. 3(b).
the former’s output is 37.8% and the latter drops to 15.5%, as depicted in Fig. 3(e).
The power extinction ratios for these two cases are 1:2.0 and 2.4:1, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's pair '2.4 and 3.9' joins the 1 mW inverted case (2.4:1) with the 2 mW first-case ratio (1:3.9); the body gives ratios of 1:2.0 and 2.4:1 at 1 mW and 1:3.9 and 3.4:1 at 2 mW. The ratios are asymmetric within each power setting.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that for two nearly-identical nanosecond pulses, the later arriving pulse is modulated by the earlier arriving one, resulting in 2.4 and 3.9 power extinction between the two, respectively, when their peak power is 1 mW and 2 mW.
quotes: For two nearly-identical nanosecond pulses, the later arriving pulse is modulated by the earlier arriving one, resulting in 2.4 and 3.9 power extinction between the two, respectively, when their peak power is 1 mW and 2 mW.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical summary of results from one device in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The body reports the 2 mW ratio of 3.9 as 1:3.9 for the Pulse 1 first case and 3.4:1 for the inverted case, so the abstract's 3.9 matches only one of the two orderings at 2 mW.

assertions.value: The authors state that the weaker modulation at 1 mW than at 2 mW is because the SFG-induced loss for each pulse is linearly reduced by half as compared to the 2-mW case, so the QZB modulation effect is reduced too.
quotes: This is because the SFG-induced loss for each pulse is linearly reduced by half as compared to the 2-mW case in Fig. 2, so that the QZB modulation effect is reduced, too.
the pulse power is scaled down to 1 mW
assertions.certainty_reason: An explanation offered by the authors without a separate test.

assertions.value: The authors state that in Fig. 3(b) a side peak appears at the end of Pulse 2 because Pulse 2 is 200 ps longer than Pulse 1, due to the limitation of their available arbitrary waveform generator. Towards the end of Pulse 1 there is not sufficient power to induce QZB for Pulse 2, so the overlapping portion of Pulse 2 experiences higher loss due to SFG, becomes critically coupled, and then returns to overcoupling further into the tail, leading to ringing.
quotes: that in Fig. 3(b), a side peak appears at the end of Pulse 2. This is because in our experiment, Pulse 2 is 200 ps longer than Pulse 1, due to the limitation of our available AWG.
towards the end of Pulse 1, there isn’t sufficient power to induce QZB for Pulse 2.
so that it returns to overcoupling, leading to the appearance of ringing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own setup, Section II, pp.3-4.
assertions.reader_inference: The two pulses are not identical in length, so the abstract's 'nearly-identical' pulses differ by 200 ps in the experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Pulse 2 output measured in Fig. 2(e) and Fig. 3(e) falls below the simulation prediction, and attribute the discrepancy to a weaker experimental cavity coupling strength for Pulse 2, as suggested by Fig. 2(c), which results in diminished power within the cavity and lower modulation efficiency.
quotes: Note that in Fig. 2(e), the experimental results for Pulse 2 fall below the simulation predictions.
This discrepancy could be attributed to a weaker experiment cavity coupling strength for Pulse 2, as suggested by Fig. 2(c)
In Fig. 3(e), the discrepancy between the simulated and measured modulation efficiencies can once again be attributed to a weaker coupling strength for Pulse 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' attribution of a model-measurement gap; no test of the cause is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulation therefore does not reproduce the inverted-order Pulse 2 data at either power level.

assertions.value: The authors state that thermo-optic and photorefractive effects are countered by fine adjustment of the phase matching condition through the lasers and the thermoelectric cooler. They state that these effects manifest at kilohertz-level response rates, and that every other pulse in the 2-MHz pulse trains does not overlap with the other pulse train and serves as a monitoring mechanism, shown in Figure 2(c, f) and 3(c, f).
quotes: the phase matching condition throughout the experiment is finely adjusted by tuning the lasers and the TEC.
These side effects, which typically manifest at kilohertz-level response rates
every other pulse in the 2-MHz pulse trains does not overlap with the other pulse train and serves as a monitoring mechanism
Figure 2(c, f) and 3(c, f) show such monitoring pulses.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental procedure, Section II, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study demonstrates an invertible optical logical circuit on chip, where the roles of control and signal are swapped by changing the relative delay between two pulses, and that strong QZB effect and all-optical modulation are observed with 10 pico-joule pulses.
quotes: This study demonstrates an invertible optical logical circuit on chip, where the roles of control and signal are swapped by changing the relative delay between two pulses.
Strong QZB effect and all-optical modulation are observed with 10 pico-joule pulses.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical conclusion from one device in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not show how 10 pJ follows from 2 mW peak power and 2 ns FWHM pulses.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results point to a new paradigm of computing circuitry and architectures, where complex functions can be realized by cascading multiple QZB gates.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.3; Section I, p.1
quotes: Our results point to a new paradigm of computing circuitry and architectures, where complex functions can be realized by cascading multiple QZB gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking author claim; no cascaded gate is built or simulated in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No cascade, truth table or multi-gate circuit is demonstrated; only one two-pulse gate is measured.

assertions.value: The authors report that when the peak power is elevated to 3 mW, both pulses induce strong second harmonic generation (SHG) whose power is measured above 100 nW at the output, and together with other stronger side effects the cavity becomes too unstable to observe the modulation effect. They state that the simplified coupled mode equations of Eqs. (1-3) fail to predict the complex interactions in the cavity.
quotes: when the peak power is elevated to 3 mW, both pulses induce strong second harmonic generation (SHG) whose power is measured above 100 nW at the output.
the cavity becomes too unstable to observe the modulation effect.
the simplified coupled mode equations in Eqs.(1-3) fail to predict the complex interactions in the cavity.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device in one study; the paper also states it as a limit of its own model.
assertions.reader_inference: The modulation was observed only at 1 mW and 2 mW; raising power above 2 mW did not improve it in this device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the modulation efficiency can be further enhanced by using a microring with steeper and smoother sidewall for higher Q-factor and with a smaller effective mode volume for stronger photon interaction, and that incorporating a drop port would allow a QZB switch where the optical paths of the pulses can be swapped by adjusting their relative delay. They state that future studies will include suppressing SHG by using further detuned laser wavelengths or changing the cross-section geometry of the microring.
quotes: the modulation efficiency can be further enhanced by using a microring with steeper and smoother sidewall for higher Q-factor
a QZB switch can be realized where the optical paths of the pulses can be swapped by adjusting their relative delay.
The future studies will include suppressing SHG by using further detuned laser wavelengths or changing the cross-section geometry of the microring
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposed next steps stated by the authors; none is tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors attribute the underlying physics to the quantum Zeno effect, and cite earlier work for counterfactual quantum computing [8], counterfactual quantum communications [9], antibunched photon-pair emission [10] and quantum Zeno blockade [11-13]. They also cite prior work for a single-photon coupling strength reaching 8.2 MHz in periodically poled TFLN microrings [18].
quotes: The underlying physics is the quantum Zeno effect, based on which counter-intuitive quantum processing can be implemented, including counterfactual quantum computing [8]
counterfactual quantum communications [9], antibunched photon-pair emission [10], and quantum Zeno blockade (QZB) [11–13].
with single-photon coupling strength reaching 8.2 MHz [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: Reference [5], cited for quantum CNOT gates, is a review of surface plasmon polariton strong coupling, so that citation does not appear to support its sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data underlying the results are not publicly available at this time but may be obtained from the authors upon reasonable request, and that the research was supported in part by the Office of Naval Research. The affiliations include Quantum Computing Inc.
